description_full: EDP, S.A. engages in the generation, transmission, distribution, and supply of electricity in Portugal, Spain, France, Poland, Romania, Italy, Belgium, the United Kingdom, Greece, Colombia, Brazil, North America, and internationally. It operates through Renewables, Networks, and Client Solutions & Energy Management segments. The company generates and sells electricity through hydro, combined-cycle gas turbine, coal, wind, solar, nuclear, and cogeneration and waste sources. The company is also involved in the supply of natural gas. In addition, it offers engineering, laboratory tests, professional training, and energy services, as well as property management services. The company was formerly known as EDP - Energias de Portugal, S.A. and changed its name to EDP, S.A. in April 2024. The company was incorporated in 1976 and is headquartered in Lisbon, Portugal.

financial_summary: EDP S A is a large-cap utilities business with a $23.3B market cap on $17.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 37%.
The company is burning through $1.1B of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 36% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Altman Z in the distress zone (0.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Utilities peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.
